The force is not right for rice yet. Keep the slider near Medium: too light leaves grains closed, while too heavy creates heat.
The grinding time is not right yet. Rice needs enough time to become fine, but overgrinding creates heat.
The force and duration are correct. Keep this process.
Rice is gentle and does not need maximum force. Try keeping the force near the middle of the slider.
Rice works best with medium force. Too light keeps the aroma closed; too heavy heats the powder and creates scorched notes.
The speed is not right for tea yet. Keep it Slow so bitterness does not rush out before the sweet return.
Slow grinding does not mean endless grinding. Too much time still builds bitterness.
The speed and duration are correct. Keep Slow and avoid sudden acceleration.
Tea needs time for the sweet return to appear. Set the grinding speed to Slow.
Tea leaf works best with slow grinding. Fast grinding releases bitterness before sweetness.
The main aroma is not clear enough. Black sesame should be higher than glutinous rice.
The paste body is covering the sesame aroma. Reduce glutinous rice so it only supports the texture.
Black sesame is suited to the main note, but too much can become bitter and dominant.
Glutinous rice is suited to support texture and smoothness, not to lead the aroma.
Peanut and black sesame have similar nutty aromas. Try placing them in the same grinding group.
Peanut blends well with sesame-like ingredients because both belong to nutty aromas.
Black sesame can blend with peanut, but it can dominate if handled too heavily.
The thick red bean aroma should form the base first. Place red bean before dried tangerine peel and rock sugar.
Dried tangerine peel is appearing too early. It should be later so bitterness does not cover the bean aroma.
Sweetness should not take the lead. Add rock sugar last to round the finish.
Red bean works well early because it builds the base body.
Dried tangerine peel works better later. Too early can release bitterness.
Rock Sugar works best at the end to round sweetness.
Sand ginger has not opened correctly yet. Use MediumHigh force, but do not push it to Heavy.
The grinding duration is not right for the salt-baked sand ginger structure yet.
The process is correct. Keep MediumHigh force and check the ratio.
Sand ginger is the core of the salt-baked powder. It must have the highest ratio.
Salt is covering the spice. Coarse salt should be the lowest support note.
Dried peel is only a light finish, but it should still be more visible than coarse salt.
Sand ginger likes MediumHigh force. Too light leaves it closed; too heavy makes it harsh.
Coarse salt should be used sparingly as support, not as the main note.
White pepper is not releasing at the right pace yet. Adjust the pestle movement to Medium speed.
The grinding duration is not right yet. Avoid overworking the sharp pepper aroma.
The speed and duration are correct. Now focus on ingredient grouping.
White pepper, peanut, and dried tangerine peel release differently. Try handling them as separate groups.
Grinding white pepper with dried tangerine peel can make spice and bitterness rush out together. Separate them.
White pepper works best at Medium speed. Too fast makes it harsh; too slow leaves it under-released.
White pepper should not be overworked with bitter or sharp ingredients such as dried tangerine peel.
Red bean should form the thickest base note, higher than glutinous rice, sesame, and lotus leaf.
Lotus leaf is a light finishing aroma. Keep it at the lowest ratio.
Glutinous rice can carry the lotus-leaf aroma. Put glutinous rice and lotus leaf in the same group.
Black sesame is too strong and can bury lotus leaf. Keep them separate.
Red bean should build the base first. Put red bean in the first position.
Lotus leaf is fragile and should appear last.
After red bean, let glutinous rice form body before adding a small amount of black sesame.
Lotus leaf works best as a very low-ratio fresh accent.
Lotus leaf can be carried by glutinous rice, but it should not be ground with strong aromas like black sesame.
Lotus leaf works best at the end. Early or heavy handling removes its fresh aroma.
Yangjiang douchi is not opening correctly yet. Use Medium force; too light stays closed and too heavy turns muddy.
Ginger is releasing at the wrong pace. Adjust the pestle movement to Medium speed.
The grinding duration is not right for the douchi structure yet.
The force, speed, and duration are correct. Continue checking ratio and order.
Yangjiang douchi must carry the savory main body, so it should have the highest ratio.
Coarse salt is only support and should stay at the lowest ratio.
Build the fermented savory base with douchi first.
Ginger works in the middle, after douchi and before the finishing peel.
Dried peel cleans the finish, while coarse salt is only a small base correction.
Yangjiang douchi likes Medium force. Too light keeps it closed; too heavy makes fermentation dull or muddy.
Yangjiang douchi can lead the savory aroma, but too much makes the structure heavy.
Ginger works best at Medium speed. Too fast makes the spice rush forward.
Ginger works well in the middle, opening freshness after the main body is established.
Sand ginger needs MediumHigh force. Too little force keeps it closed; too much makes it harsh.
Ginger needs Medium speed so the spice does not suddenly cover the sand ginger.
The whole process has gone too long or not long enough. Protect the fresh scallion finish.
Force, speed, and duration are in the target range. Submit the final aroma evaluation.
Sand ginger is the main body of the sauce and should have the highest ratio.
Coarse salt only supports the base, so it should stay at the lowest ratio.
Scallion is light, but it should still be more visible than coarse salt to leave a fresh finish.
Sand ginger and ginger can be partly ground together so the two ginger aromas connect naturally.
Scallion is fragile. Keep it separate and handle it lightly instead of grinding it with ginger.
Coarse salt can be crushed separately to form the salty base; it does not need to join the spice group.
Coarse salt should be crushed first to establish the base saltiness.
Sand ginger should establish the main body first, then ginger joins in the middle.
Scallion must be handled last so the bright green finish remains.
Sand ginger and ginger can be partly ground together so the main ginger body and fresh spice connect naturally.
Scallion white works best at the end and should not be overground with strong spicy ingredients.
